paper_title: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Discrete visual tokenization provides natural interface between image generation and autoregressive sequence modeling. By representing images as sequences of discrete symbols, visual generation can be formulated using the same next-token prediction paradigm that has driven the success of large language models [16, 46]. This formulation has also shown promise for unifying visual generation and multimodal understanding within single autoregressive architecture [36, 60]. Despite its conceptual simplicity and scalability, discrete visual autoregressive modeling faces two fundamental limitations. First, mapping continuous visual features to finite codebook introduces quantization error, 1 Figure 1 Overview of GSTAR. (a) Text-to-image generation samples spanning portraits, landscapes, typography, and structured layouts. (b) Image editing examples: given an original image and text instruction, our model produces faithful edits while preserving unrelated content (original edited). (c) Average benchmark score comparison, where our GSTAR-Pro-8B achieves competitive performance against leading proprietary, diffusion, and discrete autoregressive models. (d) Quality vs. latency at 1024 1024 resolution, where our GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B models achieve competitive quality with significantly lower latency. 2 which can discard fine-grained details and degrade reconstruction fidelity [16, 49]. The same discretization can also remove semantically relevant cues that are important for visual understanding and language alignment, reducing the informativeness of the resulting discrete representation [15, 36, 60]. Second, discrete autoregressive models generate visual tokens sequentially, making inference latency grow with sequence length [1, 46, 51, 60]. This bottleneck is amplified at high resolutions, where the number of tokens grows quadratically with image side length, widening the latency gap with diffusion models that update all spatial positions in parallel at each denoising step [22, 43]. Increasing the spatial compression rate offers direct way to reduce the number of global autoregressive steps. However, aggressive spatial compression forces each spatial token to encode more information [8, 9], exacerbating the information loss introduced by discrete quantization [16, 49]. To mitigate this loss, we adopt multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) [28, 36, 54], which represents each spatial token with multiple discrete codes and thereby expands its representation capacity. More importantly, MCQ admits useful scaling property: as detailed in Section 4.2, jointly scaling the spatial compression rate and the number of codes per token can preserve the total nominal information budget while reducing the number of global autoregressive steps. We systematically study how code scaling affects reconstruction, generation, and semantic representation, and find that it enables high-compression tokenizers at 32 and even 64well beyond the common 16 settingwhile retaining high fidelity and providing an efficient interface for downstream generation. Multi-codebook quantization requires each global autoregressive step to predict group of codes. RQTransformer-style causal depth decoders model their dependencies, but their latency grows linearly with group size and can dominate the global backbone under aggressive compression [28]. Parallel and masked-token predictors remove this serial cost [3, 5, 31, 40, 51], yet sample the codes independently and may combine incompatible modesa failure known as multi-modal collision [12]. We therefore introduce lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder: most layers run in parallel, while only the final layer retains causal path for intra-group conditioning. This keeps group-scaling overhead nearly flat without sacrificing generation quality. We evaluate our approach on large-scale text-to-image generation using five representative benchmarks: GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench. Our models perform competitively with leading systems across these benchmarks while supporting spatial compression ratios from 32 to 64. Controlled studies further examine how group scaling affects reconstruction fidelity, generation quality, and semantic representation, and compare the qualitylatency trade-off among causal, parallel, and semiautoregressive intra-group decoders. At 1024 1024 resolution, our model delivers 20 speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models and generates each image in 2.5 seconds on single NVIDIA H200. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We systematically study how scaling the group size affects reconstruction, generation, and semantic understanding under 32 and 64 spatial compression, showing that scaling the per-step capacity preserves strong representation quality with short global sequence. We propose lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder for efficiently modeling intra-group dependencies, together with an optimized inference implementation. Our system generates 1024 1024 image in 2.5 seconds on single NVIDIA H200. We further validate the effectiveness of our approach at 32 and even effective 64 spatial compression by training two models, GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, respectively, in large-scale text-to-image setting. Our models achieve performance competitive with leading models across Qwen-Image-Bench, PRISM, DPG-Bench, GenEval, and LongText-Bench, while our approach delivers 20 inference speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models.

sections.title: 2.1 Discrete Image Generation
sections.content: Discrete generators learn distributions over quantized visual tokens [16, 46, 49]. Recent advances include next-scale prediction in VAR, Infinity, and NextFlow [21, 47, 60], randomized generation orders in RAR and RandAR [41, 57], and parallel decoding in PAR and BitDance [1, 51]. Janus-Pro and Emu3.5 scale discrete generation within unified multimodal systems [11, 13]; UniAR further combines shared visual tokenizer with parallel bitwise prediction [42]. GLM-Image pairs autoregressive visual-token prediction with diffusion image decoder [59]. Representation capacity is another key axis. RQ-Transformer, MAGVIT-v2, GSQ, UniTok, and WeTok explore residual, binary, or grouped quantization [28, 36, 50, 56, 63], while BAR and BitDance model large binary token spaces with masked-bit and diffusion heads, respectively [1, 58]. Building on these advances, we study spatialgroup co-scaling at 32 and effective 64 compression, jointly examining reconstruction, semantic representation, and the trade-off of group decoding.

sections.title: 2.2 Discrete Diffusion for Accelerated Generation
sections.content: MaskGIT and Muse accelerate image generation through iterative parallel unmasking [3, 4]. Show-o combines discrete diffusion with autoregressive language modeling [53], while Emu3.5 adapts pretrained autoregressive models to parallel image-token prediction via DiDA [13]. NVIDIAs Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Image advances this direction with token editing and grouped cross-entropy for large-vocabulary image synthesis [31]. For speculative language decoding, DFlash uses block-diffusion drafting [5], whereas DSpark combines parallel backbone with lightweight sequential module to model intra-block dependencies [12]. Inspired by these approaches, we accelerate intra-group code generation by computing representations for all group slots in parallel, while using lightweight single-layer causal Transformer to model dependencies among codes.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: Multi-codebook quantization. Multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) represents each spatial token with multiple discrete codes. We instantiate MCQ with product quantization (PQ), implemented as group-wise quantization, for its simplicity and favorable scaling: increasing the number of groups consistently improves reconstruction fidelity (Sec. 5.2.1) [26, 36, 50, 63]. Specifically, PQ partitions the projected feature zt RC into Gq disjoint channel groups and quantizes each group independently: k(g) = arg min k[K] (cid:13) (cid:13)z(g) (cid:13) e(g) (cid:13) 2 (cid:13) (cid:13) 2 , ˆzt = ConcatGq g=1 e(g) k(g) . (1) The resulting code tuple provides up to Gq configurations per spatial position without increasing the spatial sequence length. Depth transformer. RQ-Transformer separates the generation of residual codes into global spatial transformer and local depth transformer [28]. The global transformer summarizes preceding spatial units into context vector, while the depth transformer models the dependencies among the codes assigned to the current unit. We adopt this spatialdepth decomposition for grouped rather than residual codes; the alternative depth-modeling strategies are detailed in Sec. 4.3.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Our framework combines deeply compressed discrete tokenizer with hierarchical autoregressive generator. We use group scaling to increase the capacity of each spatial token and develop spatialgroup co-scaling principle that preserves the nominal information budget while shortening the global sequence. Building on the native 32 tokenizer, we instantiate this principle through lossless spatial packing to construct an effective 64 tokenizer. lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder then efficiently models the correlated codes within each global step. 4 Figure 2 Grouped tokenization and spatialgroup co-scaling. (a) semantic encoder maps an image to spatially compressed latent grid, and group-wise quantization represents each position with discrete codes. Lossless 2 2 packing converts the native 32 grid into an effective 64 interface, reducing the number of global autoregressive steps by four while increasing the codes per step from to 4G. (b) Jointly scaling spatial compression and group size preserves the nominal information capacity per image while shortening the global sequence.

4.1 Deeply Compressed Tokenizer for Efficient Generation
We train a discrete tokenizer that maps an image x to a compact grid of group-wise codes and reconstructs
it as ˆx, as illustrated in Fig. 2(a). Following recent visual autoencoders and tokenizers built on pretrained
semantic encoders [15, 24, 37, 55, 61], we initialize the encoder of our 32× tokenizer from Qwen-ViT [2].
The tokenizer is optimized with standard reconstruction and vector-quantization objectives. To preserve the
semantic structure of the pretrained representation after quantization, we additionally align the quantized
features with the corresponding Qwen-ViT features. Following Scale-RAE for text-to-image generation [48],
we further employ a Gram loss [18] to match second-order feature correlations between the input and its
reconstruction. The overall training objective is

sections.title: 4.2 Scaling the Group Size
sections.content: Group-wise quantization provides direct way to increase the discrete capacity assigned to each spatial token without lengthening the global sequence. This is particularly useful under aggressive spatial compression, where each remaining position must preserve more visual information. Lets denote the effective per-axis spatial compression factor and the number of codes generated at each global position. For the native 32 tokenizer, = Gq, the number of quantization groups. With fixed codebook size K, the relationships illustrated in Fig. 2(b) are Nglobal(s) = HW Btotal(s, G, K) = Nglobal Cstep = HW s2 , Cstep(G, K) = log 2 K. s2 log 2 K, (3) Here Btotal is fixed-length nominal bit budget rather than the empirical entropy or effective semantic information of the learned codes. The two variables control complementary properties. At fixed s, increasing enlarges the representation capacity without increasing the number of global autoregressive steps. Increasing shortens the global sequence quadratically. These properties motivate spatialgroup co-scaling: scaling by α and by α2 preserves Btotal while reducing the number of global steps by factor of α2. 5 Figure 3 Comparison of intra-group prediction heads. Given the backbone context ht, (a) causal autoregressive decoding captures dependencies among codes but requires repeated, expensive head evaluations, while (b) parallel prediction head is fast but ignores these dependencies, risking inconsistent code combinations. (c) Our semi-autoregressive head addresses both limitations: parallel feature generator performs the heavy computation once, and lightweight single-layer causal Transformer models dependencies during sequential sampling. Constructing the effective 64 tokenizer. Guided by this relation, we construct an effective 64 tokenizer from the native 32 tokenizer through the 2 2 spatial packing shown in Fig. 2(a). Each neighborhood of four quantized positions is packed into one global unit, increasing the codes per step from Gq to 4Gq while shortening the global sequence by factor of four. This realizes the co-scaling relation with α = 2, preserving all quantized codes without introducing additional quantization. The packed codes are restored to the native grid before image decoding. To validate this capacity analysis, we systematically vary the group size and evaluate reconstruction fidelity, semantic representation, and downstream generation in Sec. 5.2.1. The results confirm that increasing group size provides additional usable information capacity and improves representation quality. Larger code tuples, however, also increase the cost of intra-group dependency modeling, motivating the efficient depth decoder introduced next.

sections.title: 4.3 Efficient Intra-Group Modeling
sections.content: Group scaling requires each global autoregressive step to generate tuple of correlated discrete codes. common approach, following RQ-Transformer [28], is to use causal depth head to model intra-group dependencies, but its sequential decoding incurs increasing inference latency as the group size grows. Fully parallel prediction removes this serial overhead, yet sacrifices generation quality by ignoring these dependencies. To reconcile these competing objectives, we propose semi-autoregressive head that preserves causal dependency modeling while approaching the decoding speed of parallel prediction. Below, we first examine the causal and parallel alternatives, then present our design. At global decoding step t, the autoregressive backbone produces context representation ht. The intra-group head uses this context to generate codes, yt = (yt,1, . . . , yt,G), by modeling the conditional joint distribution p(yt ht). Causal Autoregressive Head. Following the spatialdepth decomposition of RQ-Transformer and its use in grouped-code generation [28, 36], causal autoregressive head predicts the codes one by one, conditioning each prediction on the global context and previously generated codes: p(yt,g ht, yt,<g). (4) pAR(yt ht) = g=1 6 This factorization preserves intra-group dependencies, but requires running the full head for each of the sequential predictions. As grows, this serial computation becomes substantial decoding bottleneck and can dominate the global backbone under aggressive compression. Parallel Prediction Head. To remove this sequential overhead, fully parallel head predicts all codes in single forward pass: pPAR(yt ht) = g=1 p(yt,g ht). (5) This removes the intra-group serial path [3, 31, 40, 51], but makes the codes conditionally independent during sampling. Since codes within group jointly describe the same visual content, independently sampled marginals may select incompatible modes, leading to multimodal collision [12]. The quality degradation motivates head that retains causal conditioning while keeping most computation parallel. Semi-Autoregressive Head. We propose semi-autoregressive head that combines parallel trunk with lightweight causal module, retaining intra-group dependencies without repeating expensive representation modeling times. Drawing architectural inspiration from the parallelsequential drafters in DFlash and DSpark [5, 12], the parallel trunk first computes representations for all group slots in one pass: lightweight, single-layer causal Transformer then generates each code conditioned on both its parallel representation and the previously sampled intra-group codes: bt,1:G = Pψ([Mask]1:G; ht). (6) pSAR(yt ht) = g= p(yt,g ht, bt,g, yt,<g). (7) The parallel trunk is evaluated only once per global position. Only the single-layer, KV-cached causal Transformer remains sequential, allowing each code to depend on previously sampled codes without repeatedly executing the full head. Experiments in Sec. 5.2.2 show that our head achieves generation quality comparable to the fully causal head with latency close to parallel prediction, while consistently outperforming the parallel head across all three quality metrics.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: Experimental setup. We develop two models: GSTAR-Pro-8B, which uses 32 tokenizer with group size = 16, and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, which uses an effective 64 tokenizer with = 32 for fast image generation. Following prior progressive-training recipes [6, 7, 14], both models are trained through pretraining, continued training (CT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with progressively increasing image resolution.Detailed tokenizer training procedures and stage-wise generator training configurations are provided in Appendix A. Both models support image generation and editing, evaluated in Sec. 5.1. We further analyze the effects of group scaling on reconstruction, generation, and semantic understanding in Sec. 5.2.1, compare the quality and latency of different prediction heads in Sec. 5.2.2, and investigate the sources of acceleration in Sec. 5.3.

sections.title: 5.1 Main Results
sections.content: We adopt GenEval [20], DPG-Bench [23], PRISM [17], LongText-Bench [19], and Qwen-Image-Bench [30] to evaluate text-to-image generation, covering compositional alignment, perceptual quality, text rendering, and broader prompt-following capabilities. We evaluate instruction-guided image editing on GEdit-Bench [32], reporting semantic consistency, perceptual quality, and overall scores for its English subset. Results for GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B are reported in Tables 1 and 5, respectively for generation and editing. Benchmark versions, sampling configurations, and evaluation protocols are detailed in Appendix C. We also evaluate the reconstruction quality of our visual tokenizers in Appendix E. 7 Table 1 Text-to-image generation results. PRISM is the English overall combined score (Qwen2.5-VL-72B judge), rescaled from 0100 to 010. LongText reports the English subset; Qwen-Image denotes Qwen-Image-Bench overall (0100).

sections.title: 5.2.2 Intra-Group Prediction Heads
sections.content: We compare the Causal AR Head, Parallel Prediction Head, and our Semi-AR Head using Qwen3-1.7Binitialized model with 32 tokenizer and = 16. All variants share the same training setting: 100k pretraining steps at fixed 512 512 resolution, sequence length of 8,192, and global batch size of 32, followed by one epoch of SFT. As shown in Table 4, our Semi-AR Head substantially reduces inference latency while maintaining generation quality comparable to the Causal AR Head. It also consistently outperforms the Parallel Prediction Head across all three quality metrics.

sections.title: 5.3 Efficiency Analysis
sections.content: Our framework enables highly compressed visual representations that shorten the global autoregressive sequence, while the Semi-AR Head reduces the latency of intra-group modeling. Together, these designs reduce decoding costs at both the global and local levels. Beyond the architectural savings, we further optimize the system-level inference pipeline. We measure per-image latency for GSTAR-Flash-1.7B generating at 1024 1024 and apply four cumulative optimizations (Figure 5). Starting from Causal AR head baseline of 22.23 s, replacing it with our Semi-AR Head reduces latency to 14.93 (1.49) by parallelizing intra-group token prediction. The remaining optimizations target the two main bottlenecks separately: the intra-group head and the LLM backbone. For the head, we first capture each global step as single CUDA graph, eliminating kernel-dispatch overhead (2.55, 5.85 s). We then fuse chains of small elementwise and reduction kernels in the sampling and normalization paths into composite Triton kernels, reducing the per-block kernel count and eliminating redundant global-memory round trips (1.74, 3.37 s). Finally, integrating the model into SGLang [62] for LLM backbone serving yields further 1.35 speedup (2.50 s). The four stages compound to an 8.9 end-to-end speedup. 9 Figure 5 Cumulative speedup breakdown for GSTAR-Flash-1.7B at 1024 1024. Starting from the Causal AR head baseline (22.23 s), each stageSemi-AR head, CUDA graph capture, fused top-k kernel, and SGLang serving contributes multiplicative savings, reaching 8.9 end-to-end.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We explore high-quality autoregressive image generation under deep spatial compression by scaling discrete token capacity. Combining grouped quantization with efficient semi-autoregressive intra-group modeling enables generation at 32 and 64 spatial downsampling. Our GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B models demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in large-scale text-to-image generation, achieving performance competitive with leading models and 20 speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models.

sections.title: A Training Details
sections.content: A.1 Model Training Initialization and optimization. We initialize GSTAR-Pro-8B from Qwen3-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B from Qwen3-1.7B. Both models share the same three-stage training schedule, consisting of pretraining (PT), continued training (CT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We use ZeRO Stage 2 throughout all three stages and optimize both models using Adam with β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.95. Training schedule. We use any-resolution training throughout all three stages, progressively increasing the image resolution. PT runs for 400k steps at 512px, followed by 100k CT steps at 1024px. Both stages use sequence length of 4,096, global batch size of 64, and learning rate of 104. SFT runs for 30k steps, mixing 1024px and 2048px images at ratio of 1:1, with sequence length of 8,192, global batch size of 32, and learning rate of 105. During SFT, image-editing and text-to-image generation data are mixed at ratio of 3:7. Table 6 summarizes the configurations shared by both models. Table 6 Training configurations shared by GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B. All stages use any-resolution training. SFT mixes the 1024px and 2048px resolution tiers at ratio of 1:1. Stage Resolution Steps Seq. length Global batch LR PT CT SFT 512px 1024px 1024px / 2048px 400k 100k 30k 4,096 4,096 8, 64 64 32 104 104 105 Training data. For PT and CT, we collect imagetext pairs from publicly available datasets, including LAION, DataComp, and JourneyDB, and regenerate their captions using Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. For SFT, we select higher-quality subset of these data and supplement it with small proportion of images regenerated using Seedream and Nano Banana 2. A.2 Tokenizer Training Initialization and objectives. We initialize the tokenizer encoder from Qwen-ViT with spatial downsampling factor of 32. For both the ImageNet ablations and text-to-image tokenizers, we use the same loss weights: λsem = 1, λgram = 10, λperceptual = 1, λvq = 1, and λcommit = 0.25. Here λperceptual weights the perceptual reconstruction loss, and λcommit weights the commitment term within the vector-quantization objective. Optimization. All tokenizers are trained with Adam using (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.95) and global batch size of 1,024. We use base learning rate of 104 for the quantizer, decoder, and other components. To preserve the pretrained semantic encoders semantic representations, we use lower learning rate of 105 for the encoder. Tokenizer configurations. For GSTAR-Pro-8B, we train 32 tokenizer with 16 quantization groups per spatial position. For GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, we train 32 tokenizer with 8 quantization groups per spatial position, then merge each 2 2 neighborhood of quantized positions to obtain an effective 64 tokenizer with 32 groups per global position. This merging operation reorganizes the quantized representation without introducing an additional quantization step. Tokenizers for text-to-image generation. We use any-resolution training for the text-to-image tokenizers. In addition to general-purpose image data, we incorporate OCR, aesthetic, and face data to improve generalization and text-rendering capabilities. Training runs for total of 200k steps. Following UniAR [42] and Emu3.5 [13], we freeze the tokenizer after training and train DiT-based visual decoder initialized from Ideogram 4 [25], conditioned on the discrete tokens produced by the frozen tokenizer. This decoder is used solely to refine visual quality. Unlike GLM-Image [59] and X-Omni [19], our decoder 15 conditions exclusively on our discrete visual tokens, without any additional textual conditioning. The ImageNet ablation settings are described separately in Appendix A.3. A.3 ImageNet Ablation Settings Tokenizer training. For the ImageNet ablations, we train the tokenizers on ImageNet for 100k steps at fixed resolution of 256 256. The loss weights, optimizer, component-wise learning rates, and global batch size follow Appendix A.2. Class-conditional generation. For the class-to-image (C2I) ablations, we train the autoregressive generator on ImageNet at 256 256 resolution using the Llama-XL architecture from LlamaGen [46]. We train for 50k steps with sequence length of 4,096, global batch size of 128, and learning rate of 4 104. All remaining hyperparameters follow the Llama-XL configuration.

sections.title: B Multimodal Understanding
sections.content: Experimental setup. We initialize the language model from Qwen3-1.7B and train on the standard LLaVAOneVision training data [29]. We compare continuous visual representations from the original Qwen3 ViT (without further training) with discrete representations produced by our f32g16 tokenizer, which uses spatial downsampling factor of 32 and 16 quantization groups per position. Results. As shown in Table 7, our discrete tokenizer achieves multimodal understanding performance comparable to continuous visual representations, with average scores of 64.7 and 64.6, respectively. These results suggest that our tokenizer largely preserves the semantic information needed for multimodal understanding despite discretization and spatial compression. Table 7 Multimodal understanding performance using continuous and discrete visual representations. Higher is better for all metrics. The average is computed over the eight listed benchmarks, with OCRBench divided by 10 to match the 0100 scale of the other scores. Benchmark Continuous Discrete (f32g16) MathVista [34] RealWorldQA [52] MMStar [10] OCRBench [33] TextVQA [45] AI2D (NO_MASK) [27] ChartQA [38] DocVQA [39] Average 45.7 60.1 45.8 676 71.3 76.7 67.4 81.9 64.6 44.5 59.3 44.7 665 71.0 78.6 69.9 82.9 64.

sections.title: C Evaluation Protocols and Additional Results
sections.content: C.1 Latency Measurement We measure batch-one generation at 1024 1024 on an NVIDIA H200 and separately report global-backbone time, total intra-group head time, image-decoder time, and end-to-end pipeline latency. All models run in BF16 precision. The software stack consists of PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.8, Triton 3.5.1, and Transformers 4.57.6. The decode loop is captured as single CUDA graph. Each configuration is warmed up for 3 iterations, then timed over 3 independent trials; we report the median latency. Sampling uses classifier-free guidance with scale of 1.8, temperature 0.5, and top-k = 1024. We report run-to-run variation with the final measurements. Matched comparisons use identical timing boundaries and implementation settings. 16 Table 8 Text-to-image generation with lossless latent packing. The configuration with 64 spatial compression and = 32 is obtained by losslessly packing the configuration with 32 spatial compression and = 8, leaving tokenizer reconstruction unchanged. PRISM is the combined score on 010 scale. Compression GenEval DPG PRISM 0.8060 0.7885 82.49 80.44 5.30 5. 8 32 32 64 Lossless Packing at 64 Spatial Compression We evaluate whether our lossless packing strategy can increase the spatial compression factor while preserving both tokenizer reconstruction and text-to-image generation performance. Starting from f32g8 (i.e., 32 spatial compression with = 8; other configurations follow the same notation), we pack each 2 2 neighborhood of spatial latent positions along the group dimension to obtain f64g32. Specifically, four spatial positions with eight groups each are rearranged into single spatial position with 32 groups. This operation is exactly invertible and neither discards nor re-quantizes any latent codes. Consequently, applying the inverse packing operation before decoding yields identical tokenizer reconstruction by construction, while reducing the number of spatial latent positions by 4. To assess the effect of packing on generation, we train the text-to-image generator with the f64g32 representation using the same training recipe as for the f32g8 baseline. The results are reported in Table 8. As shown in Table 8, the packed f64g32 representation achieves GenEval score of 0.7885, DPG score of 80.44, and PRISM score of 5.13. Compared with f32g8, it retains strong generative performance despite using 4 shorter spatial latent sequence. These results demonstrate that our lossless packing strategy enables effective text-to-image generation at 64 spatial compression factor without altering the reconstruction capability of the tokenizer.

sections.title: E Image Reconstruction Quality
sections.content: We also evaluate the reconstruction capability of our visual tokenizers on the ImageNet validation set at fixed resolution of 512 512. We report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and compare against five open-source visual tokenizers: VQGAN [16], IBQ [44], VAR [47], Open-MAGVIT2 [35], and Emu3.5 [13]. As shown in Table 9, our f32g16 tokenizer achieves the highest PSNR of 25.12 dB at 32 effective spatial compression, exceeding Open-MAGVIT2 by 1.14 dB. At 64 effective spatial compression, our f64g32 variant achieves 23.90 dB, outperforming VQGAN, IBQ, VAR, and Emu3.5 while remaining within 0.08 dB of OpenMAGVIT2. These results show that our tokenizers retain competitive reconstruction fidelity at substantially higher effective spatial compression factors. Table 9 Image reconstruction quality on the ImageNet validation set at 512 512 resolution. We report the effective per-axis spatial compression factor; for VAR it refers to the finest latent scale. Higher PSNR is better. Tokenizer VQGAN [16] IBQ [44] VAR [47] Open-MAGVIT2 [35] Emu3.5 [13] GSTAR-Tokenizer (Ours) f32g16 GSTAR-Tokenizer (Ours) f64g Spatial compression PSNR (dB) 16 16 16 16 16 32 64 22.24 23.39 23.43 23.98 23.82 25.12 23.90 We also present qualitative reconstruction examples in Figure 6, comparing the ViT decoder and the refiner for both the f32g16 and f64g32 tokenizers. The examples illustrate how the refiner improves visual detail and sharpness while preserving the overall image content. Figure 6 Qualitative reconstruction examples. From left to right: ground truth, f32g16 ViT decoder, f32g16 refiner, f64g32 ViT decoder, and f64g32 refiner. Each row shows the same example across all methods. These visual examples are shown at 1024 1024 resolution, separately from the quantitative ImageNet evaluation at 512 512.
